testName: IISER IAT - Cell: Structure and Functions (20 Questions)

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: According to the modern cell theory, which of the following statements is INCORRECT?
options: All living organisms are composed of one or more cells
The cell is the basic unit of structure and organization in organisms
All cells arise from pre-existing cells through spontaneous generation
Cells contain hereditary information (DNA) which is passed from cell to cell during cell division
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Modern Cell Theory (Schleiden, Schwann, Virchow, and later modifications) states:
• All living things are made of cells
• Cell is the basic unit of structure and function
• All cells come from pre-existing cells by division (Omnis cellula e cellula - Virchow, 1855)
• Cells contain hereditary material (DNA)
• All cells are similar in chemical composition and metabolic activities
Step 2: Statement C is INCORRECT - it mentions spontaneous generation which was disproven by Louis Pasteur and others. Cells arise from pre-existing cells, not spontaneously.
Why others are correct: (A), (B), and (D) are all correct tenets of modern cell theory.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A prokaryotic cell is discovered with the following characteristics: absence of membrane-bound nucleus, presence of 70S ribosomes, cell wall containing peptidoglycan, and circular DNA concentrated in a region called the nucleoid. Which additional feature would distinguish it as a cyanobacterium rather than a typical bacterium?
options: Presence of flagella for locomotion
Presence of chlorophyll a and phycobilins with oxygenic photosynthesis
Presence of pili for conjugation
Presence of a slime capsule for protection
questions.explanation:
Step 1: General prokaryotic features (present in most bacteria including cyanobacteria):
• No membrane-bound nucleus
• 70S ribosomes
• Peptidoglycan cell wall
• Circular DNA in nucleoid
• Flagella, pili, capsule (in many species)
Step 2: Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae) are distinguished by:
• Oxygenic photosynthesis (produce O₂)
• Chlorophyll a (primary pigment)
• Phycobilins (phycocyanin, phycoerythrin - accessory pigments)
• Photosynthetic thylakoids (not organized as chloroplasts)
Why others are wrong: (A) Flagella found in many bacteria (E. coli, Salmonella); (C) Pili found in many Gram-negative bacteria; (D) Capsule/slime layer common in many bacteria (pathogenic and non-pathogenic).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following cellular structures is found in eukaryotic cells but is ABSENT in prokaryotic cells?
options: Ribosomes involved in protein synthesis
Plasma membrane composed of phospholipid bilayer
Membrane-bound nucleus containing linear DNA with histones
Cytoplasm as the site of metabolic reactions
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Compare eukaryotic vs prokaryotic cells:
Present in both:
• Ribosomes (though different size: 80S in eukaryotes, 70S in prokaryotes)
• Plasma membrane (phospholipid bilayer with proteins)
• Cytoplasm (site of metabolism)
• DNA as genetic material
Present only in eukaryotes:
• Membrane-bound nucleus with nuclear envelope, nucleolus
• Linear chromosomes with histone proteins
• Membrane-bound organelles (mitochondria, chloroplasts, ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vacuoles)
• Cytoskeleton (microtubules, microfilaments, intermediate filaments)
Step 2: Membrane-bound nucleus with linear DNA-histone complex is the defining feature of eukaryotes.
Why others are wrong: (A), (B), and (D) are present in both cell types.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In a eukaryotic cell, the endomembrane system includes the nuclear envelope, endoplasmic reticulum, Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, vacuoles, and plasma membrane. Which statement about this system is CORRECT?
options: All components of the endomembrane system are physically continuous with each other through direct membrane connections
The endomembrane system functions in protein synthesis, modification, sorting, and transport, as well as lipid synthesis
Mitochondria and chloroplasts are integral components of the endomembrane system
The endomembrane system is only present in animal cells and absent in plant cells
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Endomembrane system features:
• Components: Nuclear envelope, ER (rough and smooth), Golgi apparatus, lysosomes, vacuoles, vesicles, plasma membrane
• Functions:
- RER: Protein synthesis (with ribosomes)
- SER: Lipid synthesis, detoxification
- Golgi: Protein modification, sorting, packaging
- Lysosomes/Vacuoles: Digestion, storage
- Vesicles: Transport between compartments
• Not physically continuous - connected via vesicle transport
• Excludes mitochondria and chloroplasts (have own membranes, not part of endomembrane system)
• Present in both animal and plant cells
Step 2: Option B correctly describes the functions.
Why others are wrong: (A) Not physically continuous - vesicles mediate transport; (C) Mitochondria and chloroplasts are excluded; (D) Present in both animal and plant cells.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The rough endoplasmic reticulum (RER) differs from the smooth endoplasmic reticulum (SER) in that:
options: RER is the primary site of lipid synthesis while SER is studded with ribosomes for protein synthesis
RER has ribosomes attached to its surface and is involved in protein synthesis and processing, while SER lacks ribosomes and is involved in lipid synthesis and detoxification
RER is connected to the nuclear envelope while SER is connected to the Golgi apparatus directly
RER is found only in animal cells while SER is found only in plant cells
questions.explanation:
Step 1: RER vs SER comparison:
RER (Rough ER):
• Studded with ribosomes (80S) on cytosolic surface
• Synthesizes proteins that are secreted, membrane-bound, or targeted to organelles
• Protein folding and initial modification (glycosylation)
• Abundant in cells secreting proteins (pancreas, plasma cells)
SER (Smooth ER):
• Lacks ribosomes - smooth appearance
• Synthesizes lipids (phospholipids, steroids)
• Detoxification of drugs and poisons (liver cells)
• Calcium storage (muscle cells - sarcoplasmic reticulum)
• Both are connected to nuclear envelope
Step 2: Option B correctly distinguishes structure and function.
Why others are wrong: (A) Reversed functions; (C) Both connected to nuclear envelope; (D) Both present in both cell types.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following biomolecules is a heteropolymer composed of amino acid monomers linked by peptide bonds?
options: Cellulose, the structural polysaccharide of plant cell walls
DNA, the genetic material carrying hereditary information
Proteins, the functional molecules including enzymes and structural components
Starch, the storage polysaccharide in plants
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Analyze each biomolecule:
(A) Cellulose - homopolymer of glucose units (β-1,4-glycosidic bonds), polysaccharide
(B) DNA - heteropolymer of nucleotides (phosphodiester bonds), nucleic acid
(C) Proteins - heteropolymer of amino acids (20 different types) linked by peptide bonds (condensation between amino and carboxyl groups)
(D) Starch - homopolymer of glucose (α-1,4 and α-1,6 glycosidic bonds), polysaccharide
Step 2: Only proteins are heteropolymers of amino acids with peptide bonds.
Why others are wrong: (A) and (D) are polysaccharides (homopolymers of glucose); (B) is nucleic acid (polymer of nucleotides, not amino acids).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The primary structure of a protein refers to:
options: The three-dimensional shape formed by interactions between multiple polypeptide subunits
The regular, repeated folding of the polypeptide chain into α-helices or β-pleated sheets stabilized by hydrogen bonds
The unique linear sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide chain linked by peptide bonds
The overall three-dimensional conformation stabilized by disulfide bonds, hydrophobic interactions, and ionic bonds
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Protein structure levels:
• Primary structure: Linear sequence of amino acids linked by peptide bonds (covalent). Determines all other levels.
• Secondary structure: Local folding into α-helices (coiled) or β-pleated sheets (folded). Stabilized by hydrogen bonds between backbone atoms.
• Tertiary structure: Overall 3D shape of single polypeptide. Stabilized by disulfide bonds (covalent), hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, hydrophobic interactions between R-groups.
• Quaternary structure: Assembly of multiple polypeptide subunits (e.g., hemoglobin - 4 subunits).
Step 2: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence.
Why others are wrong: (A) Quaternary structure; (B) Secondary structure; (D) Tertiary structure.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: An enzyme catalyzes the conversion of substrate (S) to product (P) by lowering the activation energy. Which statement about enzyme kinetics is CORRECT?
options: The active site of an enzyme is a rigid, pre-formed structure that exactly matches the substrate shape (lock-and-key model)
According to the induced fit model, the enzyme's active site is flexible and changes shape upon substrate binding to form the enzyme-substrate complex
Enzymes are consumed during the reaction and must be regenerated after each catalytic cycle
The maximum reaction rate (Vmax) is achieved when all substrate molecules are bound to the enzyme
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Enzyme characteristics and models:
• Lock-and-key model (Fischer): Rigid active site, exact complementarity to substrate (outdated, incomplete)
• Induced fit model (Koshland, 1958): Active site is flexible, changes conformation upon substrate binding to achieve optimal fit and catalysis. More accurate.
• Enzyme properties:
- Not consumed in reaction (reusable)
- Highly specific
- Activity affected by pH, temperature, substrate concentration
• Vmax: Maximum rate when all enzyme active sites are saturated with substrate (enzyme is limiting factor)
Step 2: Induced fit model correctly describes modern understanding of enzyme-substrate interaction.
Why others are wrong: (A) Lock-and-key is outdated; active site is flexible; (C) Enzymes are NOT consumed; (D) Vmax is when all ENZYME is saturated, not substrate.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following is a secondary metabolite in plants?
options: Glucose, the primary product of photosynthesis used for energy and biosynthesis
Cellulose, the structural polysaccharide forming cell walls
Alkaloids such as morphine, nicotine, and quinine that serve defensive functions
Starch, the storage polysaccharide for energy reserve
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Metabolite classification:
Primary metabolites:
• Found in all organisms
• Essential for growth, development, reproduction
• Examples: Carbohydrates (glucose, fructose, starch, cellulose), proteins, lipids, nucleic acids, amino acids, organic acids (citric acid, acetic acid)
Secondary metabolites:
• Restricted distribution (specific taxonomic groups)
• Not essential for basic metabolic processes
• Often ecological functions (defense, attraction)
• Examples: Alkaloids (morphine, nicotine, caffeine, quinine), terpenoids (menthol, rubber), phenolics (tannins, lignin), glycosides
Step 2: Alkaloids are classic secondary metabolites.
Why others are wrong: (A), (B), and (D) are all primary metabolites essential for basic metabolism.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The DNA double helix has a diameter of approximately 2 nm, with adjacent base pairs separated by 0.34 nm along the axis. If a eukaryotic gene contains 3000 base pairs, what is the approximate length of the DNA segment in nanometers (ignoring supercoiling)?
options: 900 nm
questions.explanation:
Step 1: DNA structure parameters:
• Distance between adjacent base pairs = 0.34 nm (3.4 Å)
• Each complete turn of helix = 10 base pairs = 3.4 nm
• Diameter = 2 nm (irrelevant for this calculation)
Step 2: Calculation:
Length = Number of base pairs × Distance per base pair
Length = 3000 bp × 0.34 nm/bp
Length = 1020 nm
Or approximately 1.02 μm (micrometers)
Why others are wrong: (A) 1000 nm is approximate but 1020 is more accurate; (C) 6000 would be if each base pair was 2 nm (wrong parameter); (D) 900 is incorrect calculation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about the cell cycle is INCORRECT?
options: The cell cycle consists of interphase (G1, S, G2) and the mitotic (M) phase
DNA replication occurs during the S phase of interphase
The G1 phase is characterized by cell growth and synthesis of RNA and proteins, but no DNA synthesis
The M phase includes only mitosis (nuclear division) and excludes cytokinesis (cytoplasmic division)
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Cell cycle phases:
Interphase (longest, cell prepares for division):
• G1 phase (Gap 1): Cell growth, RNA and protein synthesis, organelle duplication, normal metabolic activities. No DNA synthesis.
• S phase (Synthesis): DNA replication, chromosome duplication (each chromosome becomes two sister chromatids), histone synthesis.
• G2 phase (Gap 2): Cell growth continues, protein synthesis (for mitosis), organelle duplication, checks for DNA errors.
M phase (Mitotic phase):
• Mitosis (nuclear division): Prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase
• Cytokinesis (cytoplasmic division): Division of cytoplasm, organelles, and cell membrane
• Both are part of M phase
Step 2: Statement D is INCORRECT - M phase includes both mitosis AND cytokinesis.
Why others are correct: (A), (B), and (C) are all accurate descriptions.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: During which stage of mitosis do the sister chromatids separate and move toward opposite poles of the cell?
options: Prophase, when chromosomes condense and the nuclear envelope breaks down
Metaphase, when chromosomes align at the metaphase plate
Anaphase, when the centromeres divide and sister chromatids are pulled apart by spindle fibers
Telophase, when nuclear envelopes re-form around the separated chromosomes
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Mitosis stages:
• Prophase: Chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes (each with two sister chromatids), nuclear envelope disintegrates, nucleolus disappears, spindle apparatus forms, centrosomes move to opposite poles.
• Metaphase: Chromosomes align at metaphase plate (equatorial plane), spindle fibers attach to kinetochores of centromeres.
• Anaphase: Centromeres divide, sister chromatids separate and become individual chromosomes, pulled to opposite poles by shortening of kinetochore microtubules. Cell elongates.
• Telophase: Chromosomes reach poles, decondense, nuclear envelope re-forms, nucleolus reappears, spindle disappears. Cytokinesis begins.
Step 2: Sister chromatid separation occurs in anaphase.
Why others are wrong: (A) Prophase - condensation, not separation; (B) Metaphase - alignment, not separation; (D) Telophase - re-formation, separation already complete.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Meiosis differs from mitosis in that:
options: Meiosis produces two genetically identical diploid daughter cells, while mitosis produces four genetically different haploid cells
Meiosis involves two sequential divisions (Meiosis I and Meiosis II) with one DNA replication, resulting in four haploid cells, while mitosis involves one division resulting in two diploid cells
Meiosis occurs only in somatic cells for growth and repair, while mitosis occurs in germ cells for reproduction
Meiosis lacks the stages of prophase, metaphase, anaphase, and telophase found in mitosis
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Compare meiosis and mitosis:
Mitosis:
• One division (prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase)
• DNA replication once, division once
• 2 diploid (2n) daughter cells genetically identical to parent
• Occurs in somatic cells (growth, repair, asexual reproduction)
Meiosis:
• Two divisions: Meiosis I (reductional) and Meiosis II (equational)
• DNA replication once (in pre-meiotic S phase), but two divisions
• 4 haploid (n) daughter cells genetically different from parent and each other
• Crossing over (prophase I), independent assortment (metaphase I)
• Occurs in germ cells (gamete formation)
Step 2: Option B correctly describes the fundamental difference in number of divisions and resulting cell ploidy.
Why others are wrong: (A) Reversed - meiosis produces 4 haploid, mitosis produces 2 diploid; (C) Reversed - meiosis in germ cells, mitosis in somatic; (D) Meiosis has same stage names (with modifications like prophase I, II).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: During meiosis I, homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) to form bivalents. What significant genetic event occurs during prophase I that contributes to genetic recombination?
options: Random segregation of sister chromatids to opposite poles
Crossing over between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes at chiasmata
Independent assortment of chromosomes at the metaphase plate
Separation of homologous chromosomes without any exchange of genetic material
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Prophase I of meiosis (longest, most complex phase):
• Leptotene: Chromosomes condense, become visible
• Zygotene: Synapsis - homologous chromosomes pair (gene for gene), form bivalents (or tetrads)
• Pachytene: Crossing over - exchange of genetic material between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes. Occurs at chiasmata (visible X-shaped structures where crossing over occurred). Creates new allele combinations.
• Diplotene: Synaptonemal complex breaks down, chiasmata visible, chromosomes begin to separate but remain attached at chiasmata
• Diakinesis: Terminalization of chiasmata, nuclear envelope breaks down
Step 2: Crossing over is the key genetic recombination event in prophase I.
Why others are wrong: (A) Sister chromatids separate in meiosis II, not I; (C) Independent assortment occurs at metaphase I, not prophase I; (D) Crossing over DOES occur, exchanging genetic material.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A cell with diploid number 2n = 6 undergoes meiosis. How many chromosomes are present in each cell at the end of meiosis I and meiosis II respectively?
options: 3 chromosomes at end of meiosis I, 3 chromosomes at end of meiosis II
6 chromosomes at end of meiosis I, 3 chromosomes at end of meiosis II
3 chromosomes at end of meiosis I, 6 chromosomes at end of meiosis II
6 chromosomes at end of meiosis I, 6 chromosomes at end of meiosis II
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Chromosome number changes in meiosis (2n = 6):
Start (before meiosis): 6 chromosomes (each with 2 chromatids after S phase)
Meiosis I (reductional division):
• Homologous chromosomes separate
• Sister chromatids remain attached at centromere
• Result: 2 cells with 3 chromosomes each (but each chromosome still has 2 chromatids)
• Ploidy reduced from 2n to n
Meiosis II (equational division, similar to mitosis):
• Sister chromatids separate
• Result: 4 cells with 3 chromosomes each (each chromosome now single chromatid)
Step 2: At end of meiosis I: 3 chromosomes; At end of meiosis II: 3 chromosomes (but chromatid number changes).
Why others are wrong: (B) 6 at end of meiosis I is wrong - reduction already occurred; (C) 6 at end of meiosis II is wrong; (D) Both wrong - ploidy is reduced.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The significance of meiosis includes all of the following EXCEPT:
options: Maintenance of constant chromosome number across generations through reduction of ploidy by half
Introduction of genetic variation through crossing over and independent assortment
Production of genetically identical daughter cells for growth and tissue repair
Creation of haploid gametes for sexual reproduction enabling restoration of diploidy at fertilization
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Significance of meiosis:
(A) Maintenance of chromosome number: Meiosis reduces 2n to n, fertilization restores 2n. Prevents doubling of chromosomes each generation. ✓
(B) Genetic variation:
• Crossing over (prophase I) - recombination between homologous chromosomes
• Independent assortment (metaphase I) - random orientation of homologous pairs
• Random fertilization - any sperm can fertilize any egg
Creates genetic diversity for evolution. ✓
(C) Genetically identical daughter cells: This is the function of mitosis, NOT meiosis. Meiosis produces genetically DIFFERENT cells. ✗
(D) Haploid gamete production: Enables sexual reproduction, diploidy restored at fertilization. ✓
Step 2: Option C describes mitosis, not meiosis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following cellular structures contains its own DNA and ribosomes, suggesting an endosymbiotic origin?
options: Nucleus and nucleolus
Mitochondria and chloroplasts
Endoplasmic reticulum and Golgi apparatus
Lysosomes and peroxisomes
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Endosymbiotic theory (Margulis, 1967):
• Mitochondria and chloroplasts originated as free-living prokaryotic organisms that were engulfed by ancestral eukaryotic cells
• Evidence:
- Own circular DNA (similar to bacterial DNA, not linear like nuclear DNA)
- Own 70S ribosomes (prokaryotic type, not 80S eukaryotic)
- Double membrane (inner from original organism, outer from host engulfment)
- Reproduce by binary fission (like bacteria), independent of cell cycle
- Size similar to bacteria (1-10 μm)
- Antibiotic sensitivity (e.g., chloroplasts sensitive to chloramphenicol)
Step 2: Mitochondria (from α-proteobacteria) and chloroplasts (from cyanobacteria) show these features.
Why others are wrong: (A) Nucleus is host structure; (C) ER and Golgi are part of endomembrane system, no own DNA; (D) Lysosomes and peroxisomes lack DNA and ribosomes.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane proposes that:
options: The membrane is a rigid, static structure composed of a lipid bilayer with proteins firmly attached to the surface
The membrane is a dynamic structure with a lipid bilayer in which proteins are embedded and can move laterally within the plane of the membrane
The membrane consists of a single layer of lipids with proteins attached on both sides
The membrane is composed entirely of proteins with lipids serving only as attachment sites
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Fluid mosaic model (Singer & Nicolson, 1972):
• Lipid bilayer: Phospholipids with hydrophilic heads (outer) and hydrophobic tails (inner) forming a double layer
• Fluid: Lipids and proteins can move laterally within their leaflet (rapid lateral diffusion, slow transverse/flip-flop)
• Mosaic: Membrane proteins are embedded in or attached to the lipid bilayer:
- Integral (intrinsic): Transmembrane, embedded within bilayer
- Peripheral (extrinsic): Attached to surface by electrostatic interactions
- Lipid-anchored: Attached via lipid molecules
• Asymmetric distribution of lipids and proteins
• Explains membrane fluidity, flexibility, protein mobility
Step 2: Option B correctly describes the dynamic, fluid nature with mobile proteins.
Why others are wrong: (A) Membrane is not rigid/static; (C) Single layer is wrong - it's a bilayer; (D) Proteins are important but lipids form the fundamental structure.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which of the following statements about ribosomes is CORRECT?
options: Prokaryotic ribosomes are 80S composed of 60S and 40S subunits, while eukaryotic ribosomes are 70S composed of 50S and 30S subunits
Ribosomes are membrane-bound organelles found only in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells
Ribosomes are composed of ribosomal RNA (rRNA) and proteins, and catalyze protein synthesis by linking amino acids via peptide bonds
Ribosomes function only in prokaryotic cells; eukaryotic cells use a different mechanism for protein synthesis
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Ribosome characteristics:
• Composition: rRNA (ribosomal RNA) + proteins (ribonucleoprotein particles)
• Prokaryotic: 70S (Svedberg units) = 50S large subunit + 30S small subunit
• Eukaryotic: 80S = 60S large + 40S small
• Location:
- Free in cytoplasm (synthesize proteins for cytosol)
- Bound to ER (synthesize secretory/membrane proteins)
- In mitochondria/chloroplasts (70S, prokaryotic type)
• Function: Protein synthesis - decode mRNA, catalyze peptide bond formation (peptidyl transferase activity is rRNA - ribozyme)
• Not membrane-bound - non-membranous organelle
Step 2: Option C correctly describes composition and function.
Why others are wrong: (A) Reversed - prokaryotic 70S, eukaryotic 80S; (B) Not membrane-bound, found in both cell types; (D) Both cell types use ribosomes for protein synthesis.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In a eukaryotic cell, the cytoskeleton is composed of three main types of protein filaments. Which combination correctly matches the filament type with its primary function?
options: Microtubules (25 nm) - cell shape and muscle contraction; Microfilaments (7 nm) - chromosome movement; Intermediate filaments (10 nm) - intracellular transport

Microtubules (25 nm) - chromosome segregation, intracellular transport, cell shape; Microfilaments (7 nm) - muscle contraction, cell motility, cytokinesis; Intermediate filaments (10 nm) - mechanical strength, anchoring organelles
Microtubules (25 nm) - mechanical strength; Microfilaments (7 nm) - DNA packaging; Intermediate filaments (10 nm) - protein synthesis
Microtubules (25 nm) - lipid synthesis; Microfilaments (7 nm) - nucleic acid synthesis; Intermediate filaments (10 nm) - energy production
questions.explanation:
Step 1: Cytoskeleton components and functions:
Microtubules (25 nm diameter):
• Hollow tubes of α/β-tubulin dimers
• Functions: Chromosome movement (spindle fibers in mitosis/meiosis), intracellular transport (motor proteins: kinesin, dynein on microtubule tracks), cell shape, cilia/flagella structure, centrioles
Microfilaments (7 nm, thinnest):
• Actin filaments (F-actin)
• Functions: Muscle contraction (with myosin), cell motility (amoeboid movement), cytokinesis (contractile ring), cell shape changes, mechanical support
Intermediate filaments (10 nm):
• Various proteins (keratins, vimentin, lamins, neurofilaments)
• Functions: Mechanical strength, structural support, anchoring organelles, maintaining cell integrity, tissue-specific markers
Step 2: Option B correctly matches all filament types with their functions.
Why others are wrong: (A) Functions are scrambled; (C) and (D) Functions are completely incorrect for each filament type.
